utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, we left off when we were talking about the nonsensical position of the alleged criminal enterprise to throw out the Croats from one-third of the area, whereas we see that it was quite the contrary in that third, or what you call a third of the area; it was the Serbs that were forced to leave with the greatest ethnic cleansing that was ever recorded in that entire war against Yugoslavia. And now look at these two positions: In the additional facts, number 94 and 95, points 94 and 95. You say that in April and May 1990, elections were held, the Croatian Democratic Community had the majority, won the majority vote, and then you go on to say, "Before the elections in Knin, a nationalistic Serbian Democratic Party was formed, the SDS, which advocated autonomy and later on secession." And that, as you have compiled it, should be and should go to show that it was under the influence of Belgrade, that a movement of some kind of the Serbs for criminal enterprise was set up, et cetera, et cetera. Whereas had you just from the first citizen in the street that you came across, you tried to collect and gather up information and facts, you would have seen that the Serbs in Croatia in 1990, when that party was set up and which went to the elections, the Serbs in Croatia en masse, over 90 per cent of them, voted for the League of Communists of Croatia, in fact, and not for that particular party. The League of Communists of Croatia, whose president at the time was the present Prime Minister of Croatia, Ivica Racan. And as you know, in the League of Communists in Croatia, there was an enormous number of Croats, too, many more Croats, in fact, than there were Serbs. And of course, members and other sympathisers and so on, party supporters. And that that is true is borne out by the fact that in an area where the Serbs in the majority, Banija, Kordun, Western Slavonia, Sremska the Srem Baranja region, it was the League of Communists of Croatia which won the elections and not what you're saying at all, that there was some kind of movement and especially that it was initiated, to boot, in Belgrade. Twenty-one members in the Croatian Sabor parliament were elected from the list of the League of Communists of Croatia. And it was only the Serbian Democratic Party of Knin that won in Knin, Benkovac, and Obrovac, those two small municipalities, and one more in Donji Lapac. Therefore, it is quite -- if you have the material facts before you and if you look at those facts, then there's no need for me to go into any explanation and to explain that what you're in fact saying here is not at all true, let alone later on or even before that and in the course of that process the Serbs were let go en masse from the state administration, from the police, from other services, there was a mass pogrom, there was the killing of Serbs, the burning of their houses, and so on and so forth. And when Croatia was proclaimed in mid-July and when the League of Communists of Croatia left the political scene to all intents and purposes, then it was spontaneously in that process that they joined the Serbian Democratic Party because they had nowhere else to go. They were not able to find any support or fulcrum anywhere else for their political life and that's what happened. That was quite logical at that time. The truth, then, is quite opposite to what you are claiming and putting forward here. It was the Serbs who were persecuted, in danger, under threat, and killed, and quite literally they had no chance whatsoever since that Ustasha-type regime came to the fore with Stipe Mesic and Tudjman as its leaders. Now, I'm going to use some of your sources, Western sources, not Milosevic's and Serb sources. Look at what Susan Woodward, for example, writes. She's a well-known US scientist, the Brooklyn Institution, and it is on page 107, published in 1995, 'The Balkan Tragedy' is the name of her book, in which she says the following: "The Croatian government [in English] [previous translation continues]... to protect their citizens from a vicious outburst of anti-Serb terrorism saw mixed communities of Dalmatia in interior during the summer months 1989 - 1989 - when cross zealots smashed storefronts, fire-bombed homes, and harassed and arrested potential Serb leaders. In many parts of Croatia, Serbs were expelled from jobs because of their nationality. Discrimination was not limited to this early flare-up but increased over the following years." [Interpretation] So that was the atmosphere. And the famous Croatian painter, or world renowned - he is a Croatian painter but he is of world renown, his name is Edo Murtic - in the paper Rijecki Novi List, in the year 2000 states the following: "I remember that several months before the elections in 1990 someone came very enthusiastically to me -" that was Tudjman, and he speaks about that meeting - "because he thought he would make an Augustincic of me for himself, and Augustincic was the sculptor and artist who portrayed Tito. And he started to convince me that we would do what the Ustashas and Pavelic were not able to do in 1941 for 250.000 Serbs. He said he'd pack them up, pack their coffers up and send them away. And the next 250.000 would either remain, or disappear." That is what is the truth. Now, take a look at the atmosphere that prevailed. Please look at. The Croatian Sabor Assembly on the 14th of May in 1887, passed a law on the use of the Cyrillic alphabet. On the 14th of May 1887, if you please. After the Second World War, all the constitutions of Croatia contained a constitutional position on the position of Serbs in Croatia as a constituent league entity in Croatia, both the 1947 constitution which speaks, in Article 11, that Serbs in Croatia are equal with the Croats, and in the 1943 -- 1963 constitution where it says that the Croatian people engaged in brotherhood and unity with the Serb people, and in the 1984 constitution which states that in the Socialist Republic of Croatia, the language of the Croats and Serbs are used, which is called either Croatian or Serbian, depending on the area it is spoken. So of -- since 1887 when the Croatian Sabor Assembly passed the law on the use of the Cyrillic alphabet right down the line, it was only with the advent of this pro-Nazi pound [as interpreted] authority that the new coat of arms, the chequerboard, et cetera, emblems of the puppet regime and independent autonomous State of Croatia was enforced and that the Latin script was enforced as the sole script and the Cyrillic script is done away with and abolished. After 103 years of it being in use, roughly. So we can see that it was in use for over a hundred years. And at a meeting of the Croatian Assembly, Sime Djodan, a member of parliament, said that all the citizens in Croatia were Croatians, were Croats. And in the constitution, except in the preamble, in the normative part, no mention is made of the Serbs in any context whatsoever. Article 2, paragraph 4 of the constitution says that the Croatian Assembly and people, independent and in conformity with the constitution, shall take decisions, et cetera, et cetera. So it is the Croatian Sabor Assembly and the Croatian people which are mentioned, which means that they are -- have -- they were entering a nationalistic hysteria. That was the atmosphere that prevailed. Look at the holidays that were proclaimed. The Croats had the right to celebrate their birthday for two of their -- Christmas for two days and the Serbs only one day. The same was true for Easter, and the same applied to the Jews; Jews that did not form part of that community had no right to celebrate their holidays. Look at the other laws, the addendum to the law on the government of Croatia. This is the sole law in Europe which enables executive organs to disband legally-elected representatives of the government and power and authority because the government of Croatia was authorised to undertake measures towards municipalities that did not toe the line, and they meant the Serbs there. Then we have the law on the Academy of Sciences, Article 1, the Croatian Academy of Science and Culture - and I'm skipping over some passages - is the legal follower of the Croatian Academy from 1941 to 1945. It inherited it and that was the legal follower from the times of Naziism. There is nothing on the law of the press, nothing about the Cyrillic script, and the Italians, Czechoslovaks, Ukrainians, et cetera, are mentioned but there is no mention made of the Serbs at all because they have been wiped out from the constitution. Look at the 4th of October Sabor meeting in 1990. So before any kind of conflicts broke out whatsoever, just a few quotations. At that particular meeting - and these are quotations from Damir Mejovsek, an MP: "I don't believe Serbs even when they bear gifts." Stjepan Sulimanac: "The people that have come to live after 1918 in Croatia and have gained some property there, a law should be passed to protect ourselves from people of that kind." Ivan Milas, another case in point: "With your -- we shall answer and respond to your rights with a brandished sabre." And this all went on in parliament. Andjelko Pavlovic: "All Serbs should be isolated," he said, "just like Iraq isolated the Kurds and set up a blockade. He is calling for a ghetto for the Serbs in 1990. And the Ustasha Ambassador Omrcanin, in Berlin, during Hitler's time, in Slobodni Tjednik, a Croatian paper, says in March: "No pogrom of the Serb people by the Croats existed, especially not in Jasenovac because this was all something that the Jews fabricated."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked by the interpreters to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] After 73 years, after the Serbian occupation of Croatia, there was freedom. So Josip Broz Tito, who was a Croat, Krajacic, Kardelj, and so on and so forth, they called this "the Serb occupation." And one of the leaders of the HDZ party, Praljak, right at the outset, on the 28th of April, 1990, writes the following -- and the elections had not been held yet. The HDZ was not in power yet. And he says: "People are already singing outside that we'll do away with the Serbs." And so on and so forth. I have to keep track of the time, but I have lots more orders and decisions that were passed from 1945 onwards for war crimes, people who were found guilty, and their set pensions, double the time they spent in prison. So when you take a look at this general atmosphere that prevailed, all I'm going to ask you: Is it the Serbs that incited and encouraged the Serbs? Who can say that? Is it -- was it Belgrade? Can you really say that? Bosiljko Misetic, the Minister of Justice in the second Croatian government in the paper Slobodna Dalmacija, on the 16th of September, 1992, and again in the Vjesnik paper, says: "A child, before it learns to read and write, ought to be taught who its enemies are, and its enemies in these areas are the Serbs," and so on and so forth. Take a look now at what their Dalmatian newspaper writes. It is an opposition paper. I think it was actually, it might still be. And this was on the 24th of April, 2001. It writes the following: "It was late autumn of 1991, and in Croatia, there was a free hunting season for the Serbs. Mercep and the others produced mass corpses in the manufacture of death in Pakracka Poljana where they were on a rampage, taking people out of their homes, out of their houses, and passing the death sentence on them by shooting them in the head on Mount Sljeme, which is a hill near Zagreb. Norac, Oreskovic, and their followers at that same time employed similar methods with the Serbs in Gospic. In Zadar, spectacular Crystal Nights, as they were called, were organised during which tens of thousands of houses were burnt and the owners had the wrong chromosomes and blood sets; they were not Croats. And the Novi List paper on the 22nd of January 2002, also a Croatian source - so I'm just quoting your own sources and Croatian sources - states the following. It says that the leadership of Croatia knew about the liquidation of the Serbs in 1991 because in a report that was sent in to Tudjman and Mesic, they all knew that. Josip Manolic, Boljkovac, et cetera. Unequivocally, it's stated: "There is certain evidence and facts on the unlawful arrests of peaceful citizens of the Serb ethnic group which are taken away and nobody knows whether they are alive or dead." So, gentlemen, those, then, are your sources. And I think that it is quite clear to everybody just how erroneous the qualifications that have been made are. And the picture that is trying to be painted here, that with democratic conditions prevailing in Croatia, there were these nationalistic Serbs. And The New York Times, in April 1997, wrote that Croatian fascism came back from its eternal hunting ground, and called upon the Western powers - USA, France, Germany, et cetera - to implement urgent measures to stop the revamping of fascism in Croatia. And then they conclude -- I have to skip a part. "Did the West perhaps become sufficiently ill in order to allow Croatian fascism to live a life after death?" On the 8th of December, 1993, The New York Times says: [in English] "The government of Croatia has forced thousands of its enemies from their homes and from the country, according to the new Zagreb office of human rights organisation. The actions have been directed mostly against Serbs who once constituted a sizeable minority in Croatia, but also against Croats opposed to the rule of President Tudjman. Since 1999 -- 1991, the Croatian authorities have blown up or razed ten thousand houses, mostly of Serbs, but also houses of Croats. In some cases, they dynamited homes with the families inside; whole families were killed. "Minister Mate Granic, Foreign Minister, in May, had acknowledged the destruction of 7.000 houses. So far, the justice authorities have investigated about 100. One hundred cases of dynamiting. But there have been no prosecution. Altogether, about 280.000 Croatian Serbs have fled the country." [Interpretation] Then The New York Times asks itself in this article: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... that the Serbs, the indigenous people and majority people, so one-third of communist Tito-created Croatia had to accept." [Interpretation] That's what I'm asking you. You should answer that question. And then blame the Serbs for not having agreed to be slaughtered as they were in 1941. And all this started in 1989 as the Brooklyn Institution wrote, namely Susan Woodward. It started in 1989, 1990, 1991, et cetera. And the conclusion is: [in English] "By expelling 280.000 Serbs, the Nazi Croat practically expelled all Serbs that they had under their control as early as 1993." [Interpretation] Which is correct, because the other half was in Krajina and Croatia, did not have that under their control, and they threw them out during the ethnic cleansing operation in which they were assisted by the Americans. Look at this. The American Jewish Committee: [In English] [Previous translation continues]... "memory, prosperity, property, restitution, and related issues confronting the Jewish communities of Central and Eastern Europe; Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Republic, Estonia." September 7 [Interpretation] this year. Ivo Goldstein, representative of Croatia, University of Zagreb, says: [In English] "There is the influence of extremist Croatian political émigrés who never broke off from the Ustasha movement. It was, therefore, necessary to dissociate the Ustasha movement from the odious image of faithful Nazi fascist ally and perpetrator of the worst kind of genocide and crimes against the civilian population during the Second World War. Instead, the intent was to provide the Ustasha with at least some kind of legitimate basis for participating in Croatia's civic development in the predominantly democratic European political environment. This was -- this was shown to be impossible without radically revising history and denying or falsify facts." [Interpretation] That is precisely what that side across the well is trying to do, to deny and falsify the facts and history. All of these things that they would have to know, they know full well. I don't have time now, but I'm asking you to look at the Encyclopedia Britannica sections that refer to that. I'm asking you to look at references in the Encyclopedia of Nations, and so on and so forth, all the sections pertaining to that. And there are different explanations provided there. In all fairness, this was published before this new Orwellian "Ministry of the Truth" gave orders to satanise the Serbs. After this order came, of course other explanations came as well. I don't have time to go into all of that. You mentioned Vukovar yesterday. In February 1991, at a meeting of the HDZ for Trpinjska Cesta [phoen] in Bordna Nasadic [phoen], Vekic, Glavas were there, and Mercep was the man in charge, the murder that you saw in that film. Cleansing Croatia from the Serbs. Cleansing. I spoke in London and at various international conferences and at various meetings that are all on film that ethnic cleansing is the greatest crime of all regardless of who commits it. Cleansing all of Croatia. Cleansing Vukovar. And then in the following order, replacing ethnic Serbs from all posts in the municipality, intimidating the Serbs until they leave the territory of the municipality, and the last state, the physical liquidation of those against which the previous measures did not succeed. And here it just says the Serbs, the Serbs, the Serbs, Milosevic are guilty. Milosevic made a speech in Kosovo on the 600th anniversary of the battle of Kosovo. And I read it here. And you see that it's quite contrary to what had been claimed. But nobody's really interested in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. facts, not to mention the fact that the government not only did not act in accordance with the Vance-Owen plan, that is to say, an agreement with the UN, but on several occasions they tried to abuse the plan, and primarily the fact that the JNA withdrew from the territory of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, according to that plan. And the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina carried out a demilitarisation. And then there are attacks at the Miljevac Plateau, the Maslenica Bridge, the Medak Pocket, Divoselo, and later, massacres of citizens and the well-known Flash and Storm operations. But let's just take a brief look at Bosnia as well. This most prominent form of that campaign of theirs, in addition to what we saw those Mujahedin doing there, I'm going to show something else to you now. During the war, it had assumed the largest proportions, that is to say, shooting their own people and then planting their own crime to the other side. In order to extort a decision by the Security Council to impose sanctions, they had needed to find a pretext. And before TV cameras, they organised a massacre of civilians in the bread line in the Vase Miskina Street in Sarajevo. This was immediately ascribed to the Serbs, and it was immediately established that this was done by the Muslims. And everything that has been written since speaks that this was done by the Muslims. The Independent newspaper already wrote in that year that the most horrible crimes, including the death of 16 civilians in the bread line, were committed by the Muslims themselves in order to obtain public support. CNN also, Corriere Della Sera and La Repubblica, dated the 23rd of August, 1992, they refer to "the abominable double game of the Muslims that makes the war in Bosnia even more cruel," pointing out that the bread line massacre was committed by the Muslims. Corriere Della Sera says that: "Everything indicates that the defenders of Sarajevo, the Croats and the Muslims, organised several attacks against their own citizens in the hope that in this way that they are going to deepen the drama of Sarajevo and the blame will only be cast on the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we were on good terms, Holbrooke said to me that Izetbegovic managed to play the role of a victim and that he, Holbrooke, called that - I remember his words - "ruthless ingeniosity." However, this not ingenious at all. This is just heartless; sacrificing thousands of his own citizens in order to be able to accuse the Serbs. I have to rush on. I have a map here. I'll give it to you. Camps for Serbs from 1991 to 1996. They existed at different points in time. Some went on for a longer period of time, some shorter. There were 778 of them altogether; 536 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, 221 in Croatia. And here is a list of every one of these camps. It includes many pages. There are many crimes that were committed. I won't have time. I won't have time to show this. Many crimes were committed in Croatia before the independence of Croatia was proclaimed, before it was recognised. There is a great number of crimes committed in Bosnia before the proclamation of independence, before recognition. Please, could you just place these two images on the overhead projector -- or three, perhaps. These two, rather. Take a look at this. Please put these two on the overhead projector. I'm not going to put any other pictures on the overhead projector. These are crimes from the 26th of March, 1992, in Sijekovac. The units crossed the Sava River and slaughtered the Serbs. Please put the big picture on the overhead projector. That's it. That's what they did. That's what the Mujahedin did, the ones we saw yesterday. And we saw Izetbegovic reviewing them yesterday. What's the matter? Is it not on the screens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's on the screen. Do you want the next photograph shown?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I haven't seen it on the screen. I only see you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's on our screen. Make sure you've got the right button.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. You don't want to show this. You don't want to show this to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is on our screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not on the screens that the public sees. Right. I see it on this screen now. But this internal screen only. So he is holding a head, the head of a Serb that he cut off. So those are the 20.000 Mujahedin that were brought to the European theatre of war through Clinton's policy, and most of them remained there and some went to America and to other countries, and they went all around Europe. And then when they start beheading your own people in wars to come, then you will know what this is all about. There are many photographs of major crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The usher is by the overhead projector. Do you want some other photographs shown to us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have time, Mr. May. I have 12 minutes left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- according to your shortened procedure. But I want to say one thing to you. For example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the usher -- there's no need for the usher to remain there. Give the photographs back, if you would, to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put the other picture on the ELMO, please, the one with the three heads. Take a look at this, these three heads of Serbs in an ammunition case. They cut off heads. These are the madmen that are doing things like that. And that is what Clinton's policy in Bosnia did. They were assembled in Bosnia. Look at Algeria, which is a Muslim country. How many Muslims, Algerians, did they kill so far? This has nothing do with Muslims. These are Islamic fundamentalists who are the enemies of the entire world. Not only of Christians or some others but of Muslims as well. You have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, do you want any other pictures shown?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have time, unfortunately, for any other pictures, but I do want to say one thing to you, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, let the usher take the pictures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as far as Bosnia is concerned, you can see this. This has to do with the Serb victims of Bosanska Dubica and Bosanska Gradiska, those two municipalities. For all the municipalities, there was a book that was published by the Centre for Investigating Crimes of the Association of Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and for each and every municipality significant events, victims, inevitable fate, and the perpetrators of the crimes. For each and every municipality, you have at least 100 perpetrators of these crimes. I wish to avail myself of the remaining time to say a few words about Srebrenica that was mentioned here. I have already said that I first heard about this -- I said this six months ago, when I first spoke here, that I first heard about this from Carl Bildt and that Radovan Karadzic swore to me that he didn't know a thing about this. All subsequent information corroborated that, including the subsequently published main report of the Dutch government published in April 2001. In item 10, it says quite literally: "There are no indications that the action was taken out in collaboration with Belgrade, neither in terms of political or military coordination. In this way, gentlemen, as far as I'm concerned, an end could be brought to this, but I don't want to place a full stop there. I want the truth to be revealed with regard to this insane crime, in the interest of justice. It has to be explained before the world public. The information that I have compiled so far, and there will be more to come, speaks of how Izetbegovic used Srebrenica for all kinds of manipulations and held it in -- in his own reserve for various political bargains. And you saw from the statement made by a member of his delegation in the report that was accepted by the UN with regard to the takeover of Srebrenica, the handover of Srebrenica. You saw all of this. Time will show that on the 1st of July, 1995, in the house of a Muslim, the former president of the municipality in Zvornik, where two members of the Muslim government from Sarajevo were present, the representatives of a mercenary military formation within the army of Republika Srpska but not under the command of the army of Republika Srpska but within the French intelligence service, they agreed to have this crime committed, that is to say, to abandon Srebrenica and to carry out this slaughter. All information shows that General Mladic knew nothing about this, nor General Krstic, who was sentenced here. I am personally convinced that the military honour of Mladic or Krstic would not allow them to execute civilians, let alone Mladic, Krstic, generals who throughout the war made a maximum effort to protect prisoners of war and civilians at all times. This mercenary unit was commanded by the same people who sent those same persons only one year later to Zaire so that they would protect Mobutu and crush a rebellion. This same organisation organised the purchase of arms a year later. And since I asked you to adopt a writ of disclosure, please do that. Those people who have a salary for that and have hundreds of associates, make them as Jacques Chirac and the French intelligence service and the American intelligence service and all other intelligence services, let them disclose all the facts they have on Srebrenica. The information I have available shows that the point of the agreement reached was the following: The underlying French idea was that the war in Bosnia should be ended through effective actions taken by NATO and through military engagement. As a pretext for military engagement, genocide that will be carried out by the Serbs will be made up, and the Serb negotiating side will have to deal with that. The presence of Ratko Mladic in Srebrenica will be used as a confirmation of the responsibility of the military leadership and of Mladic himself for having an indictment issued against him in The Hague by making it appear that a genocide was carried out and anathema will be placed on the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs and then the international community will take measures. The protagonists will not be prosecuted. One insignificant one, a member of the Croat detachments of death who happened to be there was accused, and then for the crimes in Srebrenica, Ratko Mladic should be accused and also the leadership of Republika Srpska headed by Radovan Karadzic. And this agreement was attended by two representatives of the Muslim government, that out of the French, General Janvier was there for sure, and this other person was said to be Morillon but this was not confirmed. There is no reliable information saying that it was Morillon. The agreement was that Srebrenica should be surrendered to the Serbs practically without any fighting, as forthwith withdraw and in that way make it possible for them to purportedly take over Srebrenica. Naser Oric is going to withdraw and award for the action will be 2 million Deutschmark. Mladic was not at that meeting. He was having lunch with those generals later on at the Likovac locality, but according to intelligence data, he did not know what the subject agreed upon was, and he didn't know that he was commanding all the units that took part in that, especially the one that was sent to Zaire later on by the same people that ordered the job to be done. Oric lives in Lukavac near Tuzla today. He has a restaurant on the lake and he destroyed more than 70 villages around Srebrenica and that he is one of the greatest criminals in the war. So let me conclude now. This is how things stand: I have just touched upon some of them, and I should like to emphasise that five peace plans were accepted by us: The Cutilheiro plan, the Vance-Owen Plan, the Vance-Stoltenberg, and the plan of the European Union and the Contact Group plan. All five plans were accepted by us. So as far as Serbia and I personally am concerned, everybody owes us -- everybody owes us recognition for the consistent struggle to attain peace instead of the accusations for war. We have received much recognition, and I personally have too, but I'm only going to quote two individuals who for a long time were -- who spent a long time in Yugoslavia, so they weren't ordinary visitors. Yasushi Akashi, one, the Assistant to the Secretary-General and his special envoy to Yugoslavia, and upon his departure, at a press conference which I did not attend - so he didn't have to address me, I was not there - he gave recognition for the role that I had played personally throughout the entire peace process during his entire mandate. And I'm going to ask Mr. Akashi to come forth here and testify. I hope he will accept my invitation. And Thorwald Stoltenberg, who also worked as the presiding person of the conference and worked in Yugoslavia for a long time. What Yusushi Akashi said at the press conference before his departure -- this was all before Dayton and I am the person most responsible for the agreement reached at Dayton and nobody can bring that into question. Thorwald Stoltenberg, on the 12th of December 1995, and I quote, said the following in Oslo. He said that: "President Slobodan Milosevic had played a key role in the peace process in the then Yugoslavia." Therefore, gentlemen, it is with the highest degree of responsibility and with all the facts at my disposal I claim before the international community that the policy of Serbia when it comes to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was directed towards peace and all its efforts were geared towards peace. The policy of Serbia was also to support Serbs in Bosnia in their hardships there because they found themselves faced with these hardships thanks to others. But it was the policy of Serbia that was geared first and foremost towards stopping the bloodshed and establishing peace, and arguments that the Serbs should live with others -- those were the arguments. The people that they had lived next to throughout that time. That is the truth. And the people from the international community are -- know that truth full well, even if they are calling for my own responsibilities and accountability for the crimes that they have perpetrated. They are asking that I be held responsible. So the tasks, gentlemen, you have before you are impossible unless you make an intervention in history. And if you -- unless you look at the facts. I have only touched upon these facts because of my limited time, but you must declare them null and void if you wish to falsify history completely. But in addition to the quite obvious intention to falsify history here, the indictment has fallen through. It is aborted. Because truth is stronger. And you, contrary to the intentions of the creators of this unlawful Tribunal, have enabled the world to get a glimpse of the truth and to start to understand the truth as it stands. And in the proceedings to come, this will be made even more evident and the truth will be victorious. Thank you. And I have not overstepped the time limits you set. Of course, that was to the detriment of a series of facts which I wished to put before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Are the Prosecution ready to call their first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. The first witness will be called by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. He has some protections, as the Court knows, and so the blinds will have to be brought down while he's brought in. While that's being done, may I mention one administrative matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. See if we can move the blinds while we're dealing with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The administrative matter relates to President Mesic, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who is coming next week. The timetable is that he is due to arrive on Monday, available to give evidence on Tuesday, Wednesday, possibly into Thursday. Therefore, this first witness, if incomplete, is one who we would ask may be, in the terminology that we've been using, wrapped around the evidence of Mr. Mesic. For obvious reasons; his time is very limited. Second point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before you go on to that, how long is it anticipated the first witness will be, in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In chief? Up to two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, of course we will look at that. If possible -- I know this is the beginning and therefore witnesses are inclined to take longer; it would be helpful if we could deal with him in rather less time than that. I've read the summary. I see there are substantial documents, but let us try and deal with him as rapidly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second point concerning Mr. Mesic's evidence relates to exhibits. All the exhibits have been provided in advance on the accused, but what I intend to do is to have lists served today to help him and to help the amici and, indeed, the Chamber, identifying exhibits in three categories: Exhibits that we expect to use in the course of his evidence, and I'll have those separately prepared in bundles for the Chamber and the other parties; exhibits that although we may not ask him to deal with in detail are exhibits that he'll nevertheless produce, he being the person able formally to produce them; and a third list of documents being documents that he is in a position to produce but that we don't forecast at this time necessarily needing to produce and we therefore don't want to burden the Court with but that are documents on which he would be able to give answers if, for example, the accused decided he wanted to ask him about them. In this way, we hope we will make life that much easier for the accused who is representing himself, but it is not a policy I will be in a position to comply with with any other future witness but this is obviously a major and important witness for the accused. So I will have those lists available by the end of the morning and I'll distribute them to the accused and to others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have several questions, but I won't take up more than one minute of your time. I saw that Mr. Wladimiroff wrote a letter of some kind to justify the -- himself with regard to the interview. According to what I have received, it seems that he will have to write another letter, because, for instance, he gave an interview to the Bulgarian papers, named Kultura, in which he explains, in response to a question, "Is there any possibility for Milosevic to be acquitted?" Mr. Wladimiroff said literally the following: [In English] "Yes. Practically no. If you have gone hunting and are in the pursuit of game with an automatic rifle, the chances of making a hit are greater. Milosevic has been indicted for what happened in a number of places in Kosovo, Bosnia and Croatia. Even if he is acquitted on half of the counts, he will be convicted on the other counts." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. He wrote you a letter, Mr. May, one of the most prominent intellectuals of Eastern Europe, academician Professor Dr. Velko Vlkanov, and he says: "In any case, it is horrifying that one of the amici curiae considered it possible to regard its proceedings as 'game hunting.'" And secondly, in the letter, he also says that it's not important whether a legal man comments but if he is a friend of the Court, then it is understood that he expresses what is contained in the heads of that Court and Tribunal and, therefore, that what is being talked about is a judgement brought in advance. You received the letter. I don't know whether you looked into it with your colleagues, but on the basis of what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we will return to this matter when the blinds are up and when we have started the witness, and we will hear from Mr. Wladimiroff --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will deal with all this when we've heard the witness, the blinds are up and the public can see. Now, let's have the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question with respect to the appearance of the witness. I think that it is untenable practice to start the examination of a witness and then interrupt it because the other side is not able to organise itself. And this isn't the first time. So why don't they move up the next witness or not start this witness if they're waiting for the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us not waste any more time. We'll see how this witness goes. It is, on the whole, better, of course, to finish the witness if we can, but there may be circumstances, particularly with witnesses from abroad, which prevent that happening. But we'll start this witness and we'll try and finish him before the next one starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the first, let's say, 20 minutes, the personal background and the political development of this witness will be discussed, and I would request to go into private session, because if we do that in the open, his identity would be revealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the matter which you raised before the witness started giving evidence and the complaint about Mr. Wladimiroff, we are awaiting the translation of the Bulgarian article. It should be with us on Monday, and we will hear you then on that. And Mr. Wladimiroff, you too should obviously have a copy of the article, the translation, and when you have, we will hear you in response to what Mr. Milosevic says.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I hope we can deal with that on Monday. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, we are now in open session, and I would like you -- want to remind you not to use your name now and not to speak about your positions that you had during the events. And just for the public record, the number has the number C-037. When was the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party, founded in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: It was founded sometime around the beginning of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did it take part in the multi-party elections in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it did take part. And it had a few MPs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So it didn't score well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was a branch founded in Western Slavonia or Slavonia at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes. The SDS was founded in Slavonia, all of Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which territories in Croatia did it cover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: It covered the area of Dalmatia, Lika, Baranja, Kordun, Slavonia, and in part it was present in Zagreb as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood my question. I was asking for the SDS Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: The SDS Slavonia operated from Kutina to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that is Eastern Slavonia and Western Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes, all of it together.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that the SDS didn't gain many mandates in the Croatian parliament. The Serbs in Croatia, whom did they vote for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: At that time, most of the Serbs voted for the League of Communists of Croatia, the Social Democratic Party of Croatia. It was then headed by Ivica Racan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You told us that you joined the SDS party. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Because the League of Communists of Croatia, the Social Democratic Party of Croatia did not understand the problems of the Serbs in Croatia, those that appeared after the first elections that were won by the HDZ, and they no longer represented the interests of the Serbs. Then there was a need to have the Serbs form a party that would articulate their needs and wishes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What were the Serbian issues in Croatia at that time? What were the needs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, it was the position of the Serbs that was concerned, because the party that won the elections spoke about the status of Serbs, about their privileges, about their high positions. The Serbs wanted to say that they want to retain the status they had, that is to say the rights that they had already enjoyed, and no party was prepared to discuss that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were the Serbs at that time in Croatia over-represented in the police and in the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Serbs in Slavonia have close links with the SDS leaders in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: They did with Jovan Raskovic, but not with Milan Babic and his wing of the SDS. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, Jovan Raskovic had a democratic option, an option named dialogue and negotiations. Milan Babic had become rather intolerant, narrow-minded, and he was not in favour of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was he in favour of? What were his suggestions for the solutions for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, he believed there should be an autonomy, territorial autonomy, and later he showed the wish not to be in Croatia, to break off all contacts with the Croatian government, not to have any talks with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These different goals, when did they become apparent; in which time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, sometime round the beginning of 1991, I should say, when the referendum was carried out in Croatia for secession. Mr. Babic wanted to have a referendum for annexation to Serbia, whereas the others wanted it to be a referendum for remaining in Yugoslavia. There was a drastic difference that was manifested then as far as Babic was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We come to the referendum a little bit later. The SDS in Slavonia, did they see their future within the Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did such a position of co-existence, did it have a chance exactly? Are there examples that it worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes, it did have a chance, and I think that it could have been carried through.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know an entity or an enclave called Gorski Kotar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes, I know that area also. The Serbs comprised a majority there, and it also advocated staying within Croatia. They did indeed stay within Croatia and preserved lives as well as their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This Gorski Kotar, is it part of the Krajina, the Knin region, or close to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: It is right by Krajina, right next to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there any war in this region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were there any SDS politicians active in this enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What political stance did they take; the radical one of Mr. Babic or more the Slavonian approach?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: They were more in favour of the approach that we espoused. They went to Zagreb, and they reached agreements.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And they were not harmed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Speaking of the Serbian leaders in Knin, you mentioned Mr. Babic, but was he the only one with a radical cause?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: No. There was also David Rastovic, Bosko Bozanic, Djoko Vjestica from Gradacac, and some others; Martic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they hold rallies in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How -- when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: This happened once a month, once in two months, depending on the needs they considered to be important.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which year? We're talking about which time frame?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: We are still talking about the end of 1990, the beginning of 1991, put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At such rallies, how were the Croatian government and the Croatian population portrayed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, they talked about Ustashas, the Independent State of Croatia, the events of the Second World War. That is how this was portrayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did these leaders in Knin say about the situation of the Serbian people in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, they said that they were imperiled, that they had a very hard life, that they were in danger, that they should have a state in which they should be safer, that there can be no talks or negotiations with the Croatian government, that they are extremists, that they are Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were the Serbs in danger in -- at that time in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: No. At that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We come to the details a little bit later. What was said about the Serbian state? You just mentioned the Serbs to be safe in a Serbian state. What would be the borders of that state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, as far as the people of Knin were concerned, they were satisfied if it were to be Krajina together with the Serbs from Bosnia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to discuss a map with the witness, and it's Exhibit 340, and it's tab 3 in the binder you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, this is a map of Yugoslavia, and on this map there is a line indicated. Will you please -- can you please have a look at this line and indicate it also with your pointer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is this line -- does this line say something to you? What kind of a line is it? What does it connect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: It connects the idea that Vojislav Seselj spoke about, that Serb boundaries are Karlobag, Karlovac, Virovitica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This line, was that -- in the view of Seselj, was that the new border of the Serbian state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is that the state that sometimes is referred to as Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness should answer the questions rather than have them put to him. How was that state referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Union of Serb States, or Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Seselj mention that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes, often.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which time period did you hear him say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: He said that in 1990, 1991, all the way up to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How -- how did you get knowledge of his references? You said already you heard him. Personally? Does that mean you heard him personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Through the media, in his speeches. I don't remember having heard him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The idea of the Serbs being safe in their own state, did you ever hear anything from Mr. Milosevic in this regard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: I think that this sentence was uttered a long time ago, that the Serbs should live in one state.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who -- who uttered this sentence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Usher, you can put that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've finished with that map. We should give this binder with the maps in it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 326.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said you heard it a long time ago. When did you hear Mr. Milosevic say such a remark, "All Serbs in one state"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, I think it was sometime around 1989.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On which occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: I think it was in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is that the only time that you heard him say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Perhaps one more time, later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you -- on what -- what kind of an occasion was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Referring again to Mr. Seselj, what kind of a state did he have in mind as -- in relation to the ethnic composition of such a state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: He meant a state that would include the Serbs, and as far as the Croats were concerned, it would be best for them to go to Croatia. That is to say that it would be a state of Serbs only.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he also make references -- you said he made reference to the Croats. Did he make references to other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: He talked about the Muslims, Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did he say about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, he said that Albanians should live in Albania. I can't remember what he said about Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak up or come closer to microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, you have to come closer to the microphone or speak a little bit louder. What was the media coverage that Mr. Seselj got during the time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, he was extensively covered in the press and radio, television. All the speeches he made were covered. Journalists followed him everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that also include state-owned media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And about which years? During which years did that happen that he was followed and broadcast a lot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: In 1991 most of all. 1992, 1993, and onwards as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When his comments appeared in the media, were such quotes commented upon and criticised by the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: There was no criticism. There weren't any special comments. He was given full freedom to speak. The only ones who criticised him were the independent media.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are -- were you now talking about the media as such or does that refer to the media in Belgrade and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: The media in Belgrade and Serbia. That's what we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which, if you compare the state-owned media and the independent media, how much -- how much publicity did the independent media have as compared to the state-owned media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Very limited, the independent media, especially TV. It was confined only to a part of Belgrade, perhaps. As for the newspapers, again they did not have sufficient funds, so that was very limited. As far as I know, this was just a small number of publications.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic criticise Seselj for his radical speeches? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: I never heard that. I heard about something later, but this was in 1996, 1997 when there was something.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you hear in 1996, 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, that's when elections were held in Yugoslavia. Seselj accused Milosevic for the fall of Krajina. And then Milosevic accused Seselj because of his extremist ideas.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What about the other officials in Belgrade; high-ranking, presidents and members or other Serb officials? Did they criticise or reject Seselj's ideas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: I never heard any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the situation got heated, did the Belgrade media try to calm down the situation in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have the point. Which paragraph in the summary are you dealing, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, please? I can tell you that I'm not able to find it. It may be helpful if we could just get back to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's -- actually, we are now on paragraph 19, with the Belgrade media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need to move along. Can we move along a bit more. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you always complain about having time wasted. This is indeed wasting of time. How can this witness be competent? How can he assess from his neck in the woods what the media situation is in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. He can say what he heard himself. But we'll move on from this. It is of limited assistance to us at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the authorities in Serbia support the politicians in Knin, the SDS politicians in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, the possibility was given to them to be heard through the media very often, and they were heard most of the time. I'm referring to Babic and his team.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have mentioned the idea of a Serbian -- of a state where the Serbs could be safe. What was to happen to the Serbs who lived in regions outside of these state borders that you had pointed out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, in the opinion of these persons, they should have come to live with the Serbs in Krajina and those Serb states, or if they were to stay back, then they would live in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was to happen to the non-Serbs who lived in this Serbian territory such as Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, they weren't exactly desirable in the territory of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that? Who said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, that's what Seselj said, most of all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did the leaders in Knin say, such as you mentioned them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, they said that the Croats who supported Franjo Tudjman supported an Ustasha state and were an extended arm of that, and in this way they wanted to intimidate them and that it would be best for them to live in their Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the SDS Western Slavonia at some point split from the SDS Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes, it did split from it in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Because in Eastern Slavonia, there was increasing radicalisation headed by Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which way did they get more radical?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: They established a National Council of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem which later grew into the SAO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Without any contacts with us, without reaching any kind of agreement with us, that is to say they wanted to act independently of us, and as a matter of fact, we could not really get along with them any more either.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Serbs in Western Slavonia, did they all have this political view that the situation had to be solved with negotiations or were there other people there too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: There were radical people who did not accept a policy of negotiations and dialogue, who believed that this question should be resolved radically.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did the -- how did they act towards the negotiation faction, as we can call it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: They called us the negotiators, traitors, Tudjman's men, that we were in favour of Croatia, not in favour of Serbia, that it would be best for us to leave. They threatened us. They made threats against our lives. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know the major -- the mayor of Vrgin Most, and can you tell us what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: I knew him. He was killed in 1992 in the area of the municipality of Vrgin Most. Rumour had it that he was killed by the police because he was in favour of separation from the policies of Knin, which was a very narrow-minded one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned Jovan Raskovic, that -- from Knin. What -- how did his political career develop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, he was on the rise. He was widely accepted among the populace. He knew how to speak to their hearts. He knew what they wanted and wished for. He had contacts with Babic and his people in Knin. He was in favour, though, of negotiations with Croatia. He went to see Tudjman and his associates. He was ridiculed by them. They taped conversations with him, and they took advantage of that situation. The extremists of Knin took advantage of this, too, and they turned their backs to him. So Babic established the SDS of Krajina so that he would secede from Raskovic, who was part of the original SDS, in favour of negotiations. So he created his parallel SDS which he wanted to include all of Croatia. Then after awhile, Raskovic went to Belgrade. He could not take the pressure any longer, the pressure exerted against him in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he supported by Belgrade? And by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: No he wasn't. He didn't have any support, at least as far as I was able to gather from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When Yugoslavia started to disintegrate, what was the atmosphere within the Serbian population in Croatia? Were they afraid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: The Serbs were very much afraid, the Serbs in Croatia, because it was a country in which they lived well and now they were having a Croatian state in which extremism was burgeoning and where people did not speak well of the Serbs or about their future at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were -- before the outbreak of the war, was there a mass layoff of Serbs from their positions, from their jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes. That was in Zagreb, Bjelovar, and places like that, Split and other places, that is to say, the large towns mostly, whereas where the Serbs had a majority population in Knin and Banja, they were not laid off in those regions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were the Serbs -- why were the Serbs put off -- laid off from their positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: First of all, they were laid off from the police force because the leadership wanted to reduce the number of Serb policemen and recruit their own police officers and people from their own party, and that instilled fear in the Serbs. So it started with the police force and then went on in the judiciary and the health service and in the other state organs where the Serbs had been employed up until then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were the Serbs -- before the outbreak of the war, were the Serbs expelled from Vukovar or Osijek? I'm speaking before the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: I know that there were certain incidents that took place in Vukovar, for example, and on a smaller scale in Osijek, but that was only in 1991. But I don't know about any more massive occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were Serbs, before the outbreak of the war in August 1991, were they murdered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: I heard that there were cases of that kind in Vukovar, but I heard that later on, not prior to the war itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a person Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Mercep. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he -- what do you know about him? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: What I heard was that he was in the Secretariat for National Defence of the Vukovar municipality and that with his group of like-minded men who were all extremists, that he persecuted the Serbs and that he killed them in the war, and it is to him that was ascribed the killings of Serbs in Vukovar and that he killed them in the Pakracka Poljana area, that is a region of Pakrac, in Karlovac as well, and in other parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That was during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: That was during the war, yes. And it is also believed that before the war, he engaged in frightening the Serbs in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he or his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we're going too far. The witness is giving no basis for his knowledge of these matters. It sounds like hearsay at some remove, and I don't think it really assists the Trial Chamber. Can we deal with the matters about which he has direct evidence, such as the matters in his own municipality? It may help if we came to the log revolution and began the chronology of events there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness was in a position that he knew things, and we are talking actually about something that the accused said in his opening about this person, Tomislav Mercep, and this is actually Slavonia involved here. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What did you hear Mr. Mercep say? Did you hear him say anything which is relevant to this or did you see him do anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see him do anything, no, but he did threaten the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he later -- was he investigated --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you allow this last question on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he or his men later investigated and convicted for war crimes against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: There was an investigation, but -- and trials are under way in Croatia at the moment against his men, but there was an indictment raised against the Pakracka Poljana Serb issue there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I move to the log revolution, I would like to ask this witness about a tape that he saw referring to General Spegelj, and I would kindly request to be allowed to do that because it refers to creating an atmosphere among the Serb people when all these things could happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall ever having seen a tape of the Croatian General Spegelj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes, I did see the tape. It was televised.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you -- what was said on the tape? What did Spegelj say on the tape and who made this tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: The tape was made by the army, the JNA, and Spegelj was talking about the fact that officers should be killed, that barracks should be attacked, and that general destabilisation should be caused. That's what he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how do you know that it was produced by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, that's what it said on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This tape, did it have an effect on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: It did, all of us, because suddenly there was talk of weapons, of arming men, of killing officers, of attacking barracks. So it was very disquieting. And from that time on, the Serbs looked for weapons as a form of self-defence because they were uncertain of being safe any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How was your access to Serbian media before the war and throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Before the war, we were all able to watch Yugoslav television, Serbian television from Belgrade, and Croatian and Bosnian television stations as well, and in the course of the war it was via Banja Luka that we were able to watch Serbian television stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have access to Croatian media before and during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes, we did, but it was rather difficult in Western Slavonia because there was no electricity. So it was only people who had their own generators, which were rare, that were able to follow the programmes, or transistor radios.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that the Serbs looked for weapons and for self-defence after the Spegelj tape. Did clashes break out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, there was an incident that took place in Pakrac on the 2nd of March, 1991. That was the first incident, actually. And it was a clash between the Croatian police or, rather, the ministry of the Croatian police and the police stations in Pakrac proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before we go to the Pakrac events, did you ever hear the term "log revolution" related to Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What happened in Knin? What was called the "log revolution"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, the name was given at a point when at the access roads to Knin coming in from Dalmatia, logs were placed across the road to prevent passage, or large rocks were placed on the roads to prevent access to those roads. And this began when Martic gave up the Croatian police force and any competencies and authority he had over it. And that took place on the 17th of August, 1990, when he renounced this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that this began when Martic gave up the Croatian police force. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, he no longer accepted being under the control of the police force or, rather, the ministry from Zagreb. He just worked for the Krajina police from that time on and recognised it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this access to the roads, was it re-established later on, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: The roads were not opened until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Croatian police try to get to Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, they did try but it was just not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why was it not possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: There would have been sharp clashes, like the ones at Lake Plitvice when the police wanted to place the Plitvice area under the control of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Croatian police ever attempt to take over or to get into Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: I think that they did start out towards the area but that they went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned the Pakrac events. When did the Pakrac event that you referred to take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: On the 2nd of March, 1991. That's when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what -- what did happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: There was a clash between the local police and the special forces from Zagreb, and this followed on after the disbanding of the police force which the ministry had sent to Pakrac as reinforcements. And they tried to balance out the ethnic composition, and that was the reason for which the ministry had allegedly sent a number of new policemen. So that in Pakrac, part of the police force had the old insignia, that is to say the five-pointed star, on their hats, and the new recruitments had the chequerboard insignia on their uniforms. And they said that the new policemen had taken weapons from the police station back to their homes, and the police chief asked the mayor of the town and representative of the Pakrac municipality to disband this police force so that he could call in his reserve police force which was then composed of the Serbs. And this was actually done. It was done on the 1st of March. And on the 2nd of March in the morning, the Croatian police arrived in Pakrac to assume control there and disarm that reserve police formation and to set up the police force according to and in line with the new laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was anyone killed during this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Nobody was killed during that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was reported in the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: Well, it was reported in different ways. The Serb media depicted it as if many Serbs had been killed; some Orthodox priests were mentioned. Whereas the Croatian media talked about a Serb or, rather, Chetnik rebellion, whereas, luckily, nobody had in fact been killed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How was this situation in Pakrac resolved? Was there fighting or was it resolved through negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: The situation was resolved through negotiation. Once the police had taken control, this new police force in Pakrac, the representatives of the Yugoslav army arrived in Pakrac and the Federal Ministry, and they negotiated with the representatives of the Croatian authorities from Zagreb. And there was a disarming of the reserve police force, and the weapons were turned over to the Croatian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's now move to the Plitvice events. What happened in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: What happened at Plitvice was that there was a clash between the Croatian police force, because it was an area which was held by the Serb police force up until then, so the Croatians took it over, and there was a clash between the Croatian police and the Serb police, and there were a number of dead. And Goran Hadzic and Boro Savic were arrested there. They were going from Obrovac the previous day, on their way to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did this event in Plitvice take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: On the 1st of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you yourself present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037
utterances.text: I was passing through. I had passed through several hours previously because we had the meeting in Obrovac where the large portion of the SDS had had a meeting. We discussed this for a long time, and we accepted negotiations with the Croatian authorities, and we thought that everything should be solved by peaceful means, political means. So our houses were quite nearby, so we went home, but others, like Goran Hadzic, went to spend the night in the hotel. Others were arrested, some of them were beaten up, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
